executiveSummary: A 45-minute training on writing blameless incident postmortems that people read and act on: what blameless means, the five parts in order, turning vague action items into owned, dated ones, the traps that make reviews useless, a short quiz, and a pre-publish checklist.

slides.subtitle: Incident review training · 45 minutes
slides.visualDescription: A whiteboard covered in a hand-drawn incident timeline
slides.speakerNotes: - Welcome. By the end you'll write a postmortem in an hour, not a week.

keyBullets: What a blameless postmortem is
The five parts, in order
Good and bad action items
A quick quiz
What to do on your next incident
slides.speakerNotes: - Five parts. The quiz is short and anonymous.
slides.intent: Make the time feel well spent

keyBullets: A written review of an incident that explains how the system let it happen, not who to blame
"The deploy tool allowed a config push with no review", not "Sam pushed a bad config"
slides.speakerNotes:
- The example is the whole idea in one sentence.
- Systems, not people.
slides.intent: Make the idea of blamelessness concrete

slides.slideTitle: Write it in five parts, in this order
keyBullets: Summary: what happened, in three sentences
Impact: who was affected and for how long
Timeline: what happened when, in UTC
Causes: what in the system allowed it
Actions: what we'll change, with owners
slides.speakerNotes:
- The order matters: readers stop after the summary.
- Write the summary last.

keyBullets: Timeline: every event with a timestamp
People: who was paged, and when
Root cause: the system condition, not a person
Fixes: each with an owner and a date
slides.speakerNotes: - Four things. If one is missing, the review isn't done.
slides.intent: Make the checklist easy to recall

slides.slideTitle: From incident to published review in four steps
keyBullets: Gather: pull chat logs, graphs, and the pager history
Draft: write the timeline first, the summary last
Review: one reviewer from outside the team
Publish: share it within five working days
slides.speakerNotes:
- Five working days is our standard.
- The outside reviewer catches jargon.
slides.intent: Make it feel doable in a week

slides.slideTitle: Turn a vague action item into one that gets done
keyBullets: Before: Improve monitoring of the payments service
After: Alert when payment errors exceed 1% for 5 minutes — Priya — 30 Nov
slides.speakerNotes:
- The first one will never be closed.
- The second has a threshold, an owner, and a date.

slides.slideTitle: Three traps that make reviews useless
keyBullets: Blame in disguise: "human error" as a root cause hides what the system allowed
Action items with no owner: everyone's job is nobody's job
slides.speakerNotes: - Human error is a symptom. Ask what made the error easy.

slides.subtitle: Three questions, one minute each
slides.speakerNotes: - Phones out. The link is on the screen.

keyBullets: Which is a root cause: "Sam pushed a bad config" or "config pushes skip review"?: Config pushes skip review
Who should review a postmortem?: Someone from outside the team
When should it be published?: Within five working days
slides.speakerNotes:
- Give it a minute per question.
- Most people get the first one right. The third surprises people.

keyBullets: Done: timeline with timestamps in UTC
Done: impact in numbers
Next: every action has an owner and a date
Next: one outside reviewer has read it
slides.speakerNotes: - Print this. Pin it next to your monitor.

keyBullets: Systems, not people: name what allowed it
Every action has an owner and a date
Publish within five days, while it's fresh
slides.speakerNotes: - Thank you. The template is on the wiki.
slides.intent: Make the three habits the last thing they hear
